📚 Dynamic Programming - Technique (Index Page)¶

Problem Statement: Count Number of Hops¶

A frog jumps either 1, 2, or 3 steps to go to the top. In how many ways can it reach the top of the nth step?

✅ Constraints

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵

💡 Examples Input:
n = 3

Output:
4

Explanation:
The possible ways are:

  • 1 step + 1 step + 1 step
  • 1 step + 2 steps
  • 2 steps + 1 step
  • 3 steps

🛠️ Approaches 🔁 1. Recursive Approach (Exponential Time) This approach explores all possible jumps at every step.

static int countWays(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 1;
    if (n < 0) return 0;

    return countWays(n - 1) + countWays(n - 2) + countWays(n - 3);
}

⛔ Drawback: Highly inefficient for large n due to repeated subproblems.

Code Explanation This approach uses basic recursion to explore all possible ways the frog can jump to reach step n. At each step, the frog considers jumping either 1, 2, or 3 steps. The function calls itself recursively for n-1, n-2, and n-3.

  • Base case:
    • If n == 0, it means a valid path has been found.
    • If n < 0, the path is invalid.
  • The function returns the sum of all valid paths from the current position.
  • ❗ Very inefficient for large n due to repeated computation of the same subproblems.

📦 2. Memoization (Top-Down DP) Store results of subproblems to avoid recomputation. CODE

static int countWays(int n, int[] dp) {
    if (n == 0) return 1;
    if (n < 0) return 0;
    if (dp[n] != -1) return dp[n];

    dp[n] = countWays(n - 1, dp) + countWays(n - 2, dp) + countWays(n - 3, dp);
    return dp[n];
}

Usage:

int[] dp = new int[n + 1];
Arrays.fill(dp, -1);
return countWays(n, dp);

Code Explanation This approach enhances the recursive method by storing intermediate results in a dp[] array to avoid redundant calculations.

  • Base cases remain the same.
  • Before making a recursive call, we check if the result for that value of n is already computed and stored in dp[n].
  • If so, reuse it. If not, compute and store it.
  • 🚀 Significantly improves performance by reducing time complexity to O(n).

✅ Time Complexity: O(n) ✅ Space Complexity: O(n)

📊3. Tabulation (Bottom-Up DP) Iteratively build up the result using an array.

static int countWays(int n) {
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];
    dp[0] = 1;

    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1];
        if (i >= 2) dp[i] += dp[i - 2];
        if (i >= 3) dp[i] += dp[i - 3];
    }

    return dp[n];
}

Code Explanation This iterative method builds up the solution using a table (dp[]) from the smallest subproblem (dp[0]) to the required value dp[n].

  • dp[i] represents the number of ways to reach step i.
  • For each step from 1 to n, compute dp[i] using previously computed values: dp[i-1], dp[i-2], and dp[i-3].
  • This avoids recursion completely and provides a clean bottom-up solution.

✅ Time Complexity: O(n) ✅ Space Complexity: O(n)

🔁 4. Space Optimization (Rolling Array) Only the last three values are needed at any time.

static int countWays(int n) {
    int[] ways = new int[3];
    ways[0] = 1; // n = 0
    if (n == 0) return ways[0];
    ways[1] = 1; // n = 1
    if (n == 1) return ways[1];
    ways[2] = 2; // n = 2
    if (n == 2) return ways[2];

    for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++) {
        ways[i % 3] = ways[(i - 1) % 3] + ways[(i - 2) % 3] + ways[(i - 3) % 3];
    }

    return ways[n % 3];
}

Code Explanation This approach reduces space usage by observing that only the last three values (dp[i-1], dp[i-2], dp[i-3]) are required to compute dp[i].

  • Instead of maintaining a full dp[] array, use an array of size 3 and rotate it as we iterate through steps.
  • Use modulo arithmetic (i % 3) to update and access indices cyclically.
  • 🧠 This method maintains time complexity O(n) while reducing space to O(1), making it optimal for large inputs.

✅ Time Complexity: O(n) ✅ Space Complexity: O(1)

🔚 Final Java Code (Space Optimized)

class Solution {
    static int countWays(int n) {
        int[] ways = new int[3];
        ways[0] = 1;
        ways[1] = 1;
        ways[2] = 2;

        for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++)
            ways[i % 3] = ways[(i - 1) % 3] + ways[(i - 2) % 3] + ways[(i - 3) % 3];

        return ways[n % 3];
    }
}

🧠 Summary

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Suitable For Large n
Recursion O(3^n) O(n) ❌
Memoization O(n) O(n) ✅
Tabulation O(n) O(n) ✅
Space Optimized O(n) O(1) ✅✅

Problem Statement: Ways to Reach the n’th Stair¶

There are n stairs, and a person standing at the bottom wants to reach the top. The person can climb either 1 stair or 2 stairs at a time.
Your task is to count the number of ways the person can reach the top (order matters).

✅ Constraints

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵

💡 Examples Input:
n = 4

Output:
5

Explanation:
The possible ways are:

  • 1 + 1 + 1 + 1
  • 1 + 2 + 1
  • 2 + 1 + 1
  • 1 + 1 + 2
  • 2 + 2

💠 Approaches 🔁 1. Recursive Approach (Exponential Time) Try every path by choosing to take either 1 or 2 steps recursively.

int countWays(int n) {
    if (n == 0 || n == 1) return 1;
    return countWays(n - 1) + countWays(n - 2);
}

❌ Drawback: Too slow for large n due to overlapping subproblems.

Code Explanation: This approach explores all possible paths recursively by either taking 1 or 2 steps at each stage. The base case returns 1 if the person is on step 0 or 1 (since there's only one way to stand still or take a single step).
The final result is the sum of ways to reach n-1 and n-2.

⚠️ Inefficient for large values of n because it recalculates the same subproblems multiple times, resulting in exponential time complexity.

📦 2. Memoization (Top-Down DP) Use a DP array to store results of already computed subproblems.

int countWays(int n, int[] dp) {
    if (n == 0 || n == 1) return 1;
    if (dp[n] != -1) return dp[n];

    dp[n] = countWays(n - 1, dp) + countWays(n - 2, dp);
    return dp[n];
}

Usage:

int[] dp = new int[n + 1];
Arrays.fill(dp, -1);
return countWays(n, dp);

Code Explanation: This optimizes the recursive approach by storing already computed results in a dp[] array to prevent recomputation.
Before solving a subproblem, we check if it’s already in the cache. If yes, reuse it; if not, compute and store it.
The function still uses recursion, but avoids exponential time by reusing subresults.

✅ Greatly improves performance with time complexity O(n).

✅ Time Complexity: O(n)
✅ Space Complexity: O(n)

📊 3. Tabulation (Bottom-Up DP) Fill the table iteratively starting from base cases.

int countWays(int n) {
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];
    dp[0] = 1;
    dp[1] = 1;

    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2];
    }

    return dp[n];
}

Code Explanation: This is an iterative dynamic programming approach that builds the solution from the bottom up.
We initialize a dp[] array with base values for step 0 and step 1.
Then for each step from 2 to n, compute the number of ways as the sum of the previous two values.
This avoids recursion entirely and efficiently computes the answer.

✅ Efficient and easy to understand with O(n) space and time complexity.

✅ Time Complexity: O(n)
✅ Space Complexity: O(n)

🧮 4. Space Optimization (Fibonacci Style) Only the last two results are needed to compute the next one.

int countWays(int n) {
    if (n == 0 || n == 1) return 1;

    int prev1 = 1, prev2 = 1;

    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        int curr = prev1 + prev2;
        prev2 = prev1;
        prev1 = curr;
    }

    return prev1;
}

Code Explanation: This approach further optimizes the tabulation method by using constant space.
Since the number of ways to reach step i depends only on the previous two steps, we maintain only two variables (prev1 and prev2).
We update these values in each iteration, using a rolling pattern similar to generating Fibonacci numbers.

✅ This is the most space-efficient solution with O(n) time and O(1) space.

✅ Time Complexity: O(n)
✅ Space Complexity: O(1)

🔚 Final Java Code (Space Optimized)

class Solution {
    int countWays(int n) {
        int prev1 = 1;
        int prev2 = 1;

        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
            int curr = prev1 + prev2;
            prev2 = prev1;
            prev1 = curr;
        }

        return prev1;
    }
}

🧠 Summary

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Suitable For Large n
Recursion O(2^n) O(n) ❌
Memoization O(n) O(n) ✅
Tabulation O(n) O(n) ✅
Space Optimized O(n) O(1) ✅✅

Problem Statement: Count Ways to N'th Stair (Order Does Not Matter)¶

A person is standing at the bottom of a staircase with n stairs. They can climb either 1 stair or 2 stairs at a time. You need to count how many distinct ways the person can reach the top of the stairs.

Note:

  • Order does not matter, meaning combinations like {1 2 1}, {2 1 1}, and {1 1 2} are considered the same.

✅ Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵

💡 Examples: Input:

n = 4

Output:

3

Explanation:

  • The distinct combinations are:
    • 1+1+1+1
    • 1+1+2
    • 2+2 Even though 1+2+1, 2+1+1, etc. sum to 4, they are the same as 1+1+2 due to order not mattering.

🛠️ Approaches

🔁 1. Combinatorics Based Observation

  • Since only steps of 1 and 2 are allowed and order doesn't matter, for any n, we can pick up to n / 2 twos (each two replaces two ones).
  • So the number of ways is n / 2 + 1.

📄 Code:

class Solution {
    public int nthStair(int n) {
        return (n / 2) + 1;
    }
}

Code Explanation:

  • This approach observes that when only 1-step and 2-step moves are allowed and order doesn't matter, the number of distinct combinations is determined by how many times you can use the 2-step jump.
  • Each unique combination corresponds to a different count of 2-steps (from 0 to n/2), with the remaining steps made up using 1-steps. Since the order is not considered, {1+2+1} and {2+1+1} are treated the same as {1+1+2} — hence, we don’t need to permute them.
  • The total number of such distinct combinations is simply the number of ways to choose the count of 2-steps — which is floor(n / 2) + 1.
  • This logic leads to a constant-time calculation, making the approach very efficient even for large n.

🧠 Summary Table

Value of n Possible Distinct Ways (Ignoring Order)
1 1 (1)
2 2 (1+1, 2)
3 2 (1+1+1, 1+2)
4 3 (1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 2+2)
5 3 (1+1+1+1+1, 1+1+1+2, 1+2+2)
... ...

🔢 Final Formula:

ways = (n / 2) + 1
  • 🔝 Time Complexity: O(1)
  • 🔝 Space Complexity: O(1)

This approach leverages the fact that the number of distinct unordered partitions into 1s and 2s is exactly floor(n / 2) + 1. This is efficient and ideal for large n.

Problem Statement: House Robber¶

You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed. The only constraint stopping you from robbing each of them is that adjacent houses have security systems connected, and robbing two adjacent houses will automatically notify the police. Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money in each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.

✅ Constraints

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
  • 0 <= nums[i] <= 400

💡 Examples Input: nums = [2,7,9,3,1]
Output: 12

Explanation: Rob house 1 (money = 2) + rob house 3 (money = 9) + rob house 5 (money = 1) = 2 + 9 + 1 = 12.

🛠️ Approaches 🔁 1. Recursive Approach (Exponential Time)

int rob(int[] nums, int i) {
    if (i < 0) return 0;
    return Math.max(rob(nums, i - 1), nums[i] + rob(nums, i - 2));
}

⛔ Drawback: Exponential time due to overlapping subproblems.

Code Expalnation: This approach tries every possible combination by choosing to either rob the current house and skip the next, or skip the current house and move to the next. It recursively explores both options and returns the maximum. However, this leads to repeated work and exponential time complexity as the number of overlapping subproblems grows rapidly with input size.

⛔ Not efficient for large input sizes.

📦 2. Memoization (Top-Down DP)

int rob(int[] nums) {
    int[] memo = new int[nums.length];
    Arrays.fill(memo, -1);
    return robFrom(nums, nums.length - 1, memo);
}

int robFrom(int[] nums, int i, int[] memo) {
    if (i < 0) return 0;
    if (memo[i] >= 0) return memo[i];
    memo[i] = Math.max(robFrom(nums, i - 1, memo), nums[i] + robFrom(nums, i - 2, memo));
    return memo[i];
}

Code Expalnation: Memoization solves the inefficiency of recursion by storing the results of already computed subproblems. For each house index, it calculates the maximum money that can be robbed and caches the result. If the function is called again for the same index, the result is retrieved from memory instead of recomputing.

✅ Efficient and avoids redundant computations.
✅ Suitable for moderate nums.length.

✅ Time Complexity: O(n)
✅ Space Complexity: O(n)

📊 3. Tabulation (Bottom-Up DP)

int rob(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    if (n == 1) return nums[0];

    int[] dp = new int[n];
    dp[0] = nums[0];
    dp[1] = Math.max(nums[0], nums[1]);

    for (int i = 2; i < n; i++) {
        dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i - 1], nums[i] + dp[i - 2]);
    }

    return dp[n - 1];
}

Code Expalnation: Tabulation builds the solution iteratively using a dp array where each element represents the maximum money that can be robbed up to that house. Starting from the base cases, it fills the table by choosing the max between robbing the current house + dp[i-2], or skipping it and taking dp[i-1].

✅ More space-efficient than recursion + memoization.
✅ Clear logic flow and good for understanding DP fundamentals.

✅ Time Complexity: O(n)
✅ Space Complexity: O(n)

🔁 4. Space Optimization (Two Variables)

class Solution {
    public int rob(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        if (n == 0) return 0;
        if (n == 1) return nums[0];

        int prev1 = nums[0];
        int prev2 = 0;

        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
            int take = nums[i] + prev2;
            int skip = prev1;
            int curr = Math.max(take, skip);

            prev2 = prev1;
            prev1 = curr;
        }

        return prev1;
    }
}

Code Expalnation: This approach reduces space complexity by noticing that we only need the last two computed values at any step. Instead of keeping an entire array, two variables are maintained to track the best loot up to the previous and second previous houses. The current value is computed from them, and then the variables are updated accordingly.

✅ Best space efficiency with same logic as tabulation.
✅ Ideal for large-scale input due to constant space usage.

✅ Time Complexity: O(n)
✅ Space Complexity: O(1)

🧠 Summary

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Recommended For
Recursion O(2^n) O(n) ❌
Memoization O(n) O(n) ✅
Tabulation O(n) O(n) ✅
Space Optimized O(n) O(1) ✅✅

Problem Statement: House Robber II¶

You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed. All houses at this place are arranged in a circle. That means the first house is the neighbor of the last one. Meanwhile, adjacent houses have a security system connected, and it will automatically contact the police if two adjacent houses were broken into on the same night. Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money of each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.

💡 Examples: Input:
nums = [2, 3, 2]

Output:
3

Explanation:
Robbing house 2 is the best choice, as robbing house 1 and house 3 will alert the police.

🛠️ Approach The problem is similar to the "House Robber" problem, but with a twist: since the houses are arranged in a circle, we cannot rob both the first and last houses together. Therefore, we need to solve the problem in two parts:

  • Rob houses excluding the first house.
  • Rob houses excluding the last house. Then, take the maximum of the two results.

📝 Algorithm

  1. Linear Robbery Approach:
    The approach is the same as the House Robber problem. We use dynamic programming to solve this sub-problem.

  2. Circular Robbery:
    Since the houses are arranged in a circle, we can either:

    • Rob houses starting from the first house but excluding the last house.
    • Rob houses starting from the second house but excluding the first house.

We solve both these cases and return the maximum of the two.

Code Implementation

class Solution {
    public int rob(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        if (n == 1) return nums[0];

        // Two cases: exclude the first house or exclude the last house
        return Math.max(robLinear(nums, 0, n - 2), robLinear(nums, 1, n - 1));
    }

    private int robLinear(int[] nums, int start, int end) {
        int prev1 = 0, prev2 = 0;
        for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
            int take = nums[i] + prev2;
            int skip = prev1;
            int curr = Math.max(take, skip);
            prev2 = prev1;
            prev1 = curr;
        }
        return prev1;
    }
}

🧠 Explanation:

  1. Handling Circularity:

     First, we check the base case where there is only one house (n == 1). In this case, return the money in that house.

 We then break the problem into two linear sub-problems:

     1. Rob houses from the 0th to the (n-2)th house.

     2. Rob houses from the 1st to the (n-1)th house.

 Finally, we take the maximum of these two results, since we cannot rob both the first and last house.

  2. Robbing Linear Houses: In the robLinear function, we apply the classic dynamic programming approach where prev1 represents the maximum money we can rob up to the previous house, and prev2 represents the maximum money up to two houses ago.

     For each house, we decide whether to rob it (take = nums[i] + prev2) or skip it (skip = prev1), and update prev1 and prev2 accordingly.

⏱️ Time Complexity: Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of houses (length of nums). We solve the problem in two linear passes.

Space Complexity: O(1), since we only need a constant amount of space to store the previous two values.

🧠 Space Optimization: We optimize space by keeping track of only the last two values instead of maintaining an entire DP array.

📝 Summary Table

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Suitable for Large n
Circular Robbery O(n) O(1) ✅

Problem Statement: Count the Paths¶

Given a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with V nodes labeled from 0 to V-1. Given edges, start, and destination, count the number of ways to reach from the start node to the destination node. There is a directed edge from vertex edges[i][0] to vertex edges[i][1]. Your task is to find the number of ways to reach from the start to the destination.

💡 Example: Input:

plaintext
edges = [[0, 1], [0, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]]
n = 4
start = 0
destination = 3

Output: 2 Explanation: From start = 0, the possible paths are: 0 → 1 → 3 0 → 2 → 3 Thus, the total number of paths from start to destination is 2.

🛠️ Approach The problem can be solved by using Depth-First Search (DFS) with Memoization. We perform DFS from the start node and explore all the possible paths. To avoid recomputing the same paths repeatedly, we store the result of each node in a memo array, which allows us to return the result immediately if we have already computed it for that node.

📝 Algorithm

  1. Graph Representation: Convert the list of edges into an adjacency list representation of the graph. This allows us to easily traverse all the neighbors of a node.

  2. DFS Traversal: We perform DFS starting from the start node. For each node, we explore all its neighbors and recursively count the number of paths to the destination.

  3. Memoization: Use a memo array to store the number of ways to reach the destination from each node, so we do not recompute the same result multiple times.

  4. Base Case: If we reach the destination node, return 1 because we've found a valid path.

  5. Recursive Case: For each neighboring node, recursively compute the number of paths to the destination and add them up.

Code Implementation

class Solution {
    public int possible_paths(int[][] edges, int n, int start, int destination) {
        // Step 1: Create the graph as an adjacency list
        List<List<Integer>> graph = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) graph.add(new ArrayList<>());

        // Step 2: Fill the graph with edges
        for (int[] edge : edges) {
            graph.get(edge[0]).add(edge[1]);
        }

        // Step 3: Use memoization to store the results of subproblems
        Integer[] memo = new Integer[n];
        return dfs(graph, start, destination, memo);
    }

    private int dfs(List<List<Integer>> graph, int node, int dest, Integer[] memo) {
        // Base case: If we have reached the destination, return 1
        if (node == dest) return 1;

        // If the result is already computed, return the cached value
        if (memo[node] != null) return memo[node];

        // Recursive case: Explore all the neighbors
        int count = 0;
        for (int neighbor : graph.get(node)) {
            count += dfs(graph, neighbor, dest, memo);
        }

        // Store the result in the memo array and return it
        memo[node] = count;
        return count;
    }
}

🧠 Explanation:

  1. Graph Representation: We first convert the list of edges into an adjacency list. This helps in traversing the graph easily.

  2. DFS Traversal: We start the DFS from the start node. For each node, we recursively explore its neighbors. For every valid path we reach the destination, we add 1 to the count.

  3. Memoization: Before exploring the neighbors of a node, we check if we have already computed the number of ways to reach the destination from that node. If it is already computed, we directly use the stored result to avoid recomputation.

  4. Base Case: If the current node is the destination, we return 1, indicating that we have found a valid path.

  5. Recursive Case: For each neighbor, we recursively call DFS to count the number of paths from that neighbor to the destination.

⏱️ Time Complexity: Time Complexity: O(V + E), where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges. Each node and edge is processed once due to the memoization.

Space Complexity: O(V), due to the space used by the graph and memoization array.

🧠 Space Optimization: The space complexity is already optimized with memoization, storing the results of subproblems to avoid recomputation. We are only using an additional memo array, which stores the results for each node.

📝 Summary Table

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Suitable for Large n
DFS with Memoization O(V + E) O(V) ✅

Problem Statement: Unique Paths II¶

You are given an m x n integer array grid. A robot is initially located at the top-left corner (0, 0). It tries to move to the bottom-right corner (m - 1, n - 1). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time. An obstacle and an empty space are marked as 1 and 0 respectively. A path cannot include any square with an obstacle. Return the number of possible unique paths that the robot can take to reach the bottom-right corner. The testcases are generated so that the answer will be less than or equal to 2 * 10⁹.

Example: Input:

grid = [
  [0,0,0],
  [0,1,0],
  [0,0,0]
]

Output:

2

Explanation: There are two possible paths:

  • Right → Right → Down → Down
  • Down → Down → Right → Right

Constraints:

  • m == obstacleGrid.length
  • n == obstacleGrid[i].length
  • 1 <= m, n <= 100
  • obstacleGrid[i][j] is 0 (free) or 1 (obstacle)

Approaches ✅ 1. Dynamic Programming (Tabulation)

We use a 2D dp array where dp[i][j] represents the number of unique paths to cell (i, j), taking into account obstacles.

**Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int uniquePathsWithObstacles(int[][] obstacleGrid) {
        int m = obstacleGrid.length;
        int n = obstacleGrid[0].length;

        int[][] dp = new int[m][n];

        if (obstacleGrid[0][0] == 1) return 0;
        dp[0][0] = 1;

        for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) {
            if (obstacleGrid[i][0] == 0 && dp[i-1][0] == 1)
                dp[i][0] = 1;
        }

        for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (obstacleGrid[0][j] == 0 && dp[0][j-1] == 1)
                dp[0][j] = 1;
        }

        for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) {
                if (obstacleGrid[i][j] == 0) {
                    dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1];
                }
            }
        }

        return dp[m-1][n-1];
    }
}

Code Explanation: We initialize a 2D DP array where each cell dp[i][j] stores the number of unique paths to reach cell (i, j) from the start, considering obstacles.

  • The starting point is set to 1 if there's no obstacle.
  • First row and column are filled by checking if the path to that cell is blocked.
  • Then, for each cell, if it's not an obstacle, we update dp[i][j] using dp[i-1][j] (top) and dp[i][j-1] (left).
  • Final answer is at dp[m-1][n-1].

✔️ Simple and clear.
❗ Consumes O(m * n) space.

Time Complexity: O(m * n)
Space Complexity: O(m * n)

✅ 2. Dynamic Programming (Space Optimized) We can reduce space to O(n) by keeping only the previous row.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int uniquePathsWithObstacles(int[][] obstacleGrid) {
        int m = obstacleGrid.length;
        int n = obstacleGrid[0].length;

        int[] dp = new int[n];
        dp[0] = obstacleGrid[0][0] == 0 ? 1 : 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                if (obstacleGrid[i][j] == 1) {
                    dp[j] = 0;
                } else if (j > 0) {
                    dp[j] += dp[j - 1];
                }
            }
        }

        return dp[n - 1];
    }
}

Code Explanation: Instead of a full 2D DP array, we use a 1D array dp of size n (columns). This is possible because we only need the previous row's values at any point in time.

  • Start with dp[0] = 1 if no obstacle at (0, 0).
  • Iterate over the grid row-by-row.
  • If a cell has an obstacle, set dp[j] = 0.
  • Else, update dp[j] += dp[j-1] if j > 0.
  • Result is stored in dp[n - 1].

✔️ Same logic as tabulation.
💡 Uses only O(n) space.

Time Complexity: O(m * n)
Space Complexity: O(n)

✅ 3. Recursive + Memoization We use recursion to explore all paths while caching intermediate results.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    Integer[][] memo;

    public int uniquePathsWithObstacles(int[][] obstacleGrid) {
        int m = obstacleGrid.length;
        int n = obstacleGrid[0].length;
        memo = new Integer[m][n];
        return dfs(0, 0, obstacleGrid);
    }

    private int dfs(int i, int j, int[][] grid) {
        int m = grid.length, n = grid[0].length;

        if (i >= m || j >= n || grid[i][j] == 1) return 0;
        if (i == m - 1 && j == n - 1) return 1;

        if (memo[i][j] != null) return memo[i][j];

        memo[i][j] = dfs(i + 1, j, grid) + dfs(i, j + 1, grid);
        return memo[i][j];
    }
}

Code Explanation: We define a recursive function dfs(i, j) that returns the number of paths from cell (i, j) to the bottom-right.

  • Base cases:
    • Out of bounds or obstacle → return 0.
    • Reached bottom-right → return 1.
  • Use a 2D memo array to cache results for (i, j) so each subproblem is computed only once.
  • The result is dfs(0, 0).

✔️ Intuitive and clean.
📦 Uses extra memory for memoization + recursion stack.

Time Complexity: O(m * n) (due to memoization)
Space Complexity: O(m * n) (memo + recursion stack)

❌ 4. Plain Recursion (Not Recommended) This approach leads to TLE (Time Limit Exceeded) due to exponential calls.

Code Sketch:

int dfs(int i, int j, int[][] grid) {
    if (i >= m || j >= n || grid[i][j] == 1) return 0;
    if (i == m - 1 && j == n - 1) return 1;
    return dfs(i + 1, j, grid) + dfs(i, j + 1, grid);
}

Code Explanation: This naive recursive approach explores all possible paths without caching. For every cell, it tries to move right and down recursively.

  • Very inefficient because it recalculates the same subproblems multiple times.
  • Time complexity becomes exponential (O(2^(m+n))), leading to Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) for larger grids.

🚫 Not recommended for production use.

Time Complexity: O(2^(m+n))
Space Complexity: O(m + n) (recursion stack)

Summary of Approaches

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Optimal
DP Tabulation O(m * n) O(m * n) ✅
DP Space Optimized O(m * n) O(n) ✅
Memoization (DFS) O(m * n) O(m * n) ✅
Plain Recursion Exponential O(m + n) ❌

Conclusion This problem is a classic variation of the "Unique Paths" problem that introduces obstacles. The best practice is to use bottom-up DP or top-down memoization to efficiently solve it in O(m * n) time.

Problem Statement: Count all possible paths from top left to bottom right¶

You are given a matrix of size m x n and you need to find the number of unique paths from the top-left corner (position (0, 0)) to the bottom-right corner (position (m-1, n-1)), given the constraints that from each cell, you can only move either right or down.

Input:

  • Two integers m and n representing the number of rows and columns of the matrix.

Output:

  • The number of possible paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.

Example: Input:

m = 3, n = 3

Output:

6

Explanation: The 6 unique paths in a 3 x 3 grid can be represented as:

  • Right, Right, Down, Down
  • Right, Down, Right, Down
  • Right, Down, Down, Right
  • Down, Right, Right, Down
  • Down, Right, Down, Right
  • Down, Down, Right, Right

Approaches:

1. Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up Approach)

In this approach, we use a 2D DP table to store the number of ways to reach each cell from the top-left corner. At each position (i, j) in the matrix, the number of ways to reach it is the sum of the number of ways to reach the cell directly above it (i-1, j) and the cell directly to the left of it (i, j-1).

Steps:

  1. Base Cases:

    • There is exactly one way to reach any cell in the first row (move only right). So, set dp[0][j] = 1 for all j.
    • There is exactly one way to reach any cell in the first column (move only down). So, set dp[i][0] = 1 for all i.

  2. Recursive Relation:

    • For each cell (i, j) (starting from (1, 1)), the number of ways to reach this cell is the sum of the number of ways to reach the cell directly above it and the cell directly to the left of it:
      dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]

  3. Final Result:

    • The number of unique paths to the bottom-right corner is stored in dp[m-1][n-1].

Code:

class Solution {
    int numberOfPaths(int m, int n) {
        // Initialize a 2D DP table
        int[][] dp = new int[m][n];
        
        // Set base cases: there is only one way to reach any cell in the first row or first column
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) dp[i][0] = 1;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) dp[0][j] = 1;
        
        // Fill the DP table
        for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) {
                dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]; // Total paths are the sum of top and left cells
            }
        }
        
        // The result is the number of ways to reach the bottom-right corner
        return dp[m-1][n-1];
    }
}

Explanation:

  1. Initialization: The first row and the first column are initialized to 1, because there is only one way to reach any cell in the first row (by moving right) or in the first column (by moving down).
  2. Filling the DP Table: For each cell (i, j), we compute the number of ways to reach it by adding the values of the cell directly above it (dp[i-1][j]) and the cell directly to the left of it (dp[i][j-1]).
  3. Result: The value in dp[m-1][n-1] will give the total number of unique paths from the top-left to the bottom-right.

Time Complexity:

  • O(m * n): We are iterating over every cell in the m x n matrix to compute the number of ways to reach each cell.

Space Complexity:

  • O(m * n): We are using a 2D array dp of size m x n to store the number of paths.

2. Optimized Dynamic Programming (Space Optimization)

In this optimized approach, we notice that we only need the current row and the previous row to calculate the number of paths. Thus, we can reduce the space complexity by using a 1D array instead of a 2D array.

Steps:

  1. Use a 1D array dp[] of size n.
  2. Initialize dp[0] = 1 because there is exactly one way to reach any cell in the first column.
  3. Iterate through the matrix, and at each step, update the current row based on the previous row.

Code:

class Solution {
    int numberOfPaths(int m, int n) {
        // Initialize a 1D DP array
        int[] dp = new int[n];
        
        // Set base case: there is only one way to reach any cell in the first column
        dp[0] = 1;
        
        // Fill the DP array
        for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) {
                dp[j] += dp[j-1]; // Add the number of ways to reach the cell from the left
            }
        }
        
        // The result is the value at the last column
        return dp[n-1];
    }
}

Explanation:

  • We use a 1D array dp[] to keep track of the number of ways to reach each column in the current row.
  • dp[j] += dp[j-1] ensures that we add the number of ways to reach a cell from the left column.
  • The final answer is found in dp[n-1], which represents the number of ways to reach the bottom-right corner.

Time Complexity:

  • O(m * n): We still have to iterate over the matrix, but we're using only a 1D array for storage.

Space Complexity:

  • O(n): We only use a 1D array of size n for storage.

3. Combinatorial Approach (Mathematical) The problem of counting unique paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner in a grid can also be viewed as a combinatorial problem. To get from the top-left to the bottom-right, we need to make m-1 down moves and n-1 right moves. The total number of moves is m + n - 2, and we need to choose m - 1 of those moves to be down (or equivalently, n - 1 to be right).

The number of ways to do this is given by the binomial coefficient:

C(m+n-2, m-1) = (m+n-2)! / ((m-1)! * (n-1)!)

Code:

class Solution {
    public int numberOfPaths(int m, int n) {
        // Calculate the binomial coefficient C(m+n-2, m-1)
        return factorial(m+n-2) / (factorial(m-1) * factorial(n-1));
    }
    
    // Helper method to calculate factorial
    private int factorial(int num) {
        int result = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i <= num; i++) {
            result *= i;
        }
        return result;
    }
}

Explanation:

  • The factorial method computes the factorial of a number, which is then used to compute the binomial coefficient.
  • We compute the number of unique paths using the formula: C(m+n-2, m-1).

Time Complexity:

  • O(m + n): The factorial computation takes linear time.

Space Complexity:

  • O(1): No additional space is required apart from the input parameters and a few variables.

Conclusion:

  • Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up): This is the most intuitive approach, where we fill a DP table to compute the number of ways to reach each cell.
  • Space Optimization (1D DP): This reduces the space complexity to O(n) while still keeping the time complexity at O(m * n).
  • Combinatorial Approach: This approach uses mathematical formulas to directly compute the result, which is very efficient in terms of space complexity.

Each approach has its advantages and can be chosen based on the problem constraints and requirements.

Problem Statement: Minimum Path Sum¶

You are given an m x n grid filled with non-negative numbers. Find a path from the top-left to the bottom-right corner that minimizes the sum of all numbers along the path. You can only move either down or right at any point in time.

Example Input:

grid = [
  [1,3,1],
  [1,5,1],
  [4,2,1]
]

Output:

7

Explanation: The path 1 → 3 → 1 → 1 → 1 minimizes the sum to 7.

Constraints

  • m == grid.length
  • n == grid[i].length
  • 1 <= m, n <= 200
  • 0 <= grid[i][j] <= 100

Approaches ✅ 1. Dynamic Programming (In-place Tabulation) We modify the grid in place.
Each cell contains the minimum path sum to reach that cell from the top-left.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minPathSum(int[][] grid) {
        int m = grid.length;
        int n = grid[0].length;

        for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) {
            grid[0][j] += grid[0][j - 1];
        }

        for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) {
            grid[i][0] += grid[i - 1][0];
        }

        for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) {
                grid[i][j] += Math.min(grid[i - 1][j], grid[i][j - 1]);
            }
        }

        return grid[m - 1][n - 1];
    }
}

Code Explanation: We use the input grid itself as a DP table.
Each cell is updated in-place to store the minimum path sum from the start to that cell:

  • The first row and column are initialized by accumulating values since there's only one path to each.
  • For the rest of the cells, take the minimum of the top or left neighbor and add the current cell's value.
  • The bottom-right cell will contain the final answer.

✔️ Optimal for space.
🧠 Modifies input directly, so no extra memory is used.

Time Complexity: O(m * n)
Space Complexity: O(1) (modifying input grid)

✅ 2. Dynamic Programming (Using Extra Space) Use a separate dp array to store the minimum path sum.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minPathSum(int[][] grid) {
        int m = grid.length, n = grid[0].length;
        int[][] dp = new int[m][n];
        
        dp[0][0] = grid[0][0];

        for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) dp[i][0] = dp[i - 1][0] + grid[i][0];
        for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 1] + grid[0][j];

        for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) {
                dp[i][j] = Math.min(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]) + grid[i][j];
            }
        }

        return dp[m - 1][n - 1];
    }
}

Code Explanation: We create a separate 2D DP array to store the minimum path sums:

  • dp[i][j] holds the minimum cost to reach cell (i, j).
  • Initialize first row and column by cumulative sums (as only one path exists to them).
  • For other cells, compute the minimum sum using the top and left neighbors, and add the current grid value.
  • Return the value in the bottom-right cell.

📦 Requires extra memory but preserves input.
✅ Easy to debug and understand.

Time Complexity: O(m * n)
Space Complexity: O(m * n)

✅ 3. Recursive + Memoization (Top-Down) A recursive DFS with memoization to cache subproblems.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minPathSum(int[][] grid) {
        int m = grid.length, n = grid[0].length;
        Integer[][] memo = new Integer[m][n];
        return dfs(0, 0, grid, memo);
    }

    private int dfs(int i, int j, int[][] grid, Integer[][] memo) {
        if (i >= grid.length || j >= grid[0].length) return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        if (i == grid.length - 1 && j == grid[0].length - 1) return grid[i][j];
        if (memo[i][j] != null) return memo[i][j];

        int down = dfs(i + 1, j, grid, memo);
        int right = dfs(i, j + 1, grid, memo);

        return memo[i][j] = grid[i][j] + Math.min(down, right);
    }
}

Code Explanation: This approach uses recursive DFS to explore paths, with memoization to cache intermediate results:

  • If a cell is already computed, use the cached result.
  • At each step, try moving down and right, and store the minimum path sum for each cell.
  • Base case: If out of bounds, return a large number. If at destination, return its value.
  • The recursion starts from the top-left corner and builds down to the bottom-right.

🧠 Top-down approach with smart reuse of subproblem results.
💡 Slower than tabulation but conceptually elegant.

Time Complexity: O(m * n)
Space Complexity: O(m * n) (memo + recursion stack)

❌ 4. Plain Recursion (Without Memoization) This method explores all paths and results in TLE for large grids.

Code Sketch:

int dfs(int i, int j, int[][] grid) {
    if (i >= m || j >= n) return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    if (i == m - 1 && j == n - 1) return grid[i][j];
    return grid[i][j] + Math.min(dfs(i + 1, j, grid), dfs(i, j + 1, grid));
}

Code Explanation: A naive recursive solution that tries all possible paths from top-left to bottom-right:

  • At each cell, it recursively explores moving right and down, adding the current cell value.
  • No memoization is used, so subproblems are recalculated multiple times.

🚫 Inefficient and leads to Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) on large inputs due to exponential growth in calls.

Time Complexity: O(2^(m+n))
Space Complexity: O(m + n) (recursion depth)

Summary of Approaches

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Optimal
DP (In-place) O(m * n) O(1) ✅
DP (Extra Space) O(m * n) O(m * n) ✅
Recursive + Memoization O(m * n) O(m * n) ✅
Plain Recursion Exponential O(m + n) ❌

Conclusion The optimal solution is to use in-place DP, which avoids extra space and runs in O(m * n) time.
Memoized recursion is also a good alternative for a top-down approach.

Problem Statement: Maximum Path Sum in Matrix¶

You are given a matrix mat[][] of size n x m where each element is a positive integer. Starting from any cell in the first row, you are allowed to move to the next row, but with specific movement constraints. From any cell (r, c) in the current row, you can move to any of the three possible positions:

  • (r+1, c-1) — move diagonally to the left.
  • (r+1, c) — move directly down.
  • (r+1, c+1) — move diagonally to the right.

Find the maximum sum of any path starting from any column in the first row and ending at any column in the last row, following the above movement constraints.

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n, m ≤ 1000
  • mat[i][j] ≥ 1

Example Input:

mat = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
    [7, 8, 9]
]

Output:

15

Explanation: The path with the maximum sum is 3 → 6 → 9, giving a sum of 18.

Approaches

1. Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up Approach)

The most efficient approach is to use dynamic programming. The idea is to iterate over the rows and calculate the maximum sum for each cell while considering all three possible directions of movement.

class Solution {
    public int maximumPath(int[][] mat) {
        int n = mat.length, m = mat[0].length;
        int res = Arrays.stream(mat[0]).max().getAsInt();
        
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < m; j++) {
                int up = mat[i - 1][j];
                int left = (j > 0) ? mat[i - 1][j - 1] : 0;
                int right = (j < m - 1) ? mat[i - 1][j + 1] : 0;
                mat[i][j] += Math.max(up, Math.max(left, right));
                res = Math.max(res, mat[i][j]);
            }
        }
        return res;
    }
}

Code Explanation: This approach iterates over the matrix from the second row to the last, and for each cell, it updates the value by adding the maximum possible sum from the three allowed directions in the previous row:

  • Directly above
  • Diagonally left above
  • Diagonally right above

The matrix is updated in-place, and the maximum value from the last row is returned as the result.

✔️ Most optimal in both time and space.
🚀 Efficient for large grids.

Time Complexity:

  • O(n * m) because we are iterating over the entire matrix once.

Space Complexity:

  • O(1) if we use space optimization and update the matrix in place.

2. Recursive Approach (Brute Force)

A naive approach would be to explore every possible path recursively, starting from any cell in the first row, and recursively exploring all valid paths (down, left-down, right-down) until reaching the last row.

class Solution {
    public int maximumPath(int[][] mat) {
        int n = mat.length, m = mat[0].length;
        int maxSum = Integer.MIN_VALUE;

        // Start recursion from each cell in the first row
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
            maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, findMaxPath(mat, 0, i, n, m));
        }
        return maxSum;
    }

    private int findMaxPath(int[][] mat, int r, int c, int n, int m) {
        // Base case: if we reach the last row
        if (r == n - 1) {
            return mat[r][c];
        }

        // Move to the next row in three possible directions
        int down = mat[r][c] + findMaxPath(mat, r + 1, c, n, m);
        int left = (c > 0) ? mat[r][c] + findMaxPath(mat, r + 1, c - 1, n, m) : Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        int right = (c < m - 1) ? mat[r][c] + findMaxPath(mat, r + 1, c + 1, n, m) : Integer.MIN_VALUE;

        return Math.max(down, Math.max(left, right));
    }
}

Code Explanation: This naive approach recursively explores all possible paths starting from each cell in the first row, moving to the next row in three allowed directions at every step:

  • Down
  • Diagonally left
  • Diagonally right

The recursion continues until the last row is reached, and the maximum path sum is computed from all paths.

⚠️ Highly inefficient due to recomputation of overlapping subproblems.
❌ Not feasible for large matrices (TLE risk).

Time Complexity:

  • O(3^n) as we recursively explore three paths at each step.

Space Complexity:

  • O(n) due to the recursive call stack.

3. Memoization (Top-Down DP)

The recursive approach can be optimized by using memoization to store the results of subproblems, which ensures that each subproblem is solved only once.

class Solution {
    public int maximumPath(int[][] mat) {
        int n = mat.length, m = mat[0].length;
        int maxSum = Integer.MIN_VALUE;

        // Memoization table to store intermediate results
        Integer[][] memo = new Integer[n][m];

        // Start recursion from each cell in the first row
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
            maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, findMaxPath(mat, 0, i, n, m, memo));
        }
        return maxSum;
    }

    private int findMaxPath(int[][] mat, int r, int c, int n, int m, Integer[][] memo) {
        // Base case: if we reach the last row
        if (r == n - 1) {
            return mat[r][c];
        }

        // If this subproblem has already been solved, return the result
        if (memo[r][c] != null) {
            return memo[r][c];
        }

        // Move to the next row in three possible directions
        int down = mat[r][c] + findMaxPath(mat, r + 1, c, n, m, memo);
        int left = (c > 0) ? mat[r][c] + findMaxPath(mat, r + 1, c - 1, n, m, memo) : Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        int right = (c < m - 1) ? mat[r][c] + findMaxPath(mat, r + 1, c + 1, n, m, memo) : Integer.MIN_VALUE;

        // Store the result in the memo table
        memo[r][c] = Math.max(down, Math.max(left, right));

        return memo[r][c];
    }
}

Code Explanation: This is an optimized version of the recursive approach using memoization to store and reuse results of already computed states:

  • For each call, if the result is already in the memo table, reuse it.
  • Otherwise, calculate recursively using the same three-directional rules and cache the result.

🧠 Avoids recomputation, leading to significant performance gain.
✅ Good top-down alternative to tabulation.

Time Complexity:

  • O(n * m) because we only solve each subproblem once.

Space Complexity:

  • O(n * m) for the memoization table.

4. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

In this approach, we can perform a level-order traversal (BFS) from the first row, processing all possible paths iteratively. However, this method is not as optimal as DP for problems with overlapping subproblems.

BFS Approach Concept:

  • Initialize a queue with all the positions from the first row.
  • For each node in the queue, process all its neighbors (possible moves to the next row).
  • Update the sums based on the path sums and continue until all nodes are processed.
  • At the end, return the maximum sum found in the last row.

Code Explanation: This approach uses a queue to perform level-wise traversal starting from all first-row cells:

  • At each level (row), we enqueue possible next moves for all cells in the current row.
  • For each cell, we track the path sum and update accordingly.
  • After processing all levels, the maximum sum from the last row is returned.

💡 Conceptually interesting but not as efficient as dynamic programming.
🚫 May have higher overhead and complexity than necessary.

Summary of Approaches

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Suitable For Large n
Dynamic Programming O(n * m) O(1) ✅
Recursive (Brute) O(3^n) O(n) ❌
Memoization (DP) O(n * m) O(n * m) ✅
BFS O(n * m) O(n * m) ✅

Conclusion

  • Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up) is the most efficient approach for solving this problem in both time and space.
  • Recursive (Brute Force) and Memoization are less efficient but can be useful for smaller grids.
  • Breadth-First Search (BFS) is not as efficient as DP and should be avoided for this type of problem.

Problem Statement: Triangle¶

You are given a triangle array, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom. For each step, you may move to an adjacent number of the row below. More formally, if you are on index i on the current row, you may move to either index i or index i + 1 on the next row.

Example Input:

triangle = [
     [2],
    [3,4],
   [6,5,7],
  [4,1,8,3]
]

Output:

11

Explanation: The path with minimum sum is 2 → 3 → 5 → 1 = 11.

Constraints

  • 1 <= triangle.length <= 200
  • triangle[0].length == 1
  • triangle[i].length == triangle[i - 1].length + 1
  • -10^4 <= triangle[i][j] <= 10^4

Approaches

✅ 1. Bottom-Up DP (1D Optimized) Iterate from the bottom to the top row, updating a 1D dp array in-place.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minimumTotal(List<List<Integer>> triangle) {
        int n = triangle.size();
        int[] dp = new int[n];

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            dp[i] = triangle.get(n - 1).get(i);
        }

        for (int row = n - 2; row >= 0; row--) {
            for (int col = 0; col <= row; col++) {
                dp[col] = triangle.get(row).get(col) + Math.min(dp[col], dp[col + 1]);
            }
        }

        return dp[0];
    }
}

Code Explanation: This approach initializes a 1D array (dp) with the values from the last row of the triangle. Then, it iteratively moves from the bottom to the top row, updating dp in place. For each element, it adds the current triangle value to the minimum of the two adjacent numbers in the dp array.

🟢 Optimizes space to O(n)
🚀 Most efficient solution in terms of space usage

Time Complexity: O(n^2)
Space Complexity: O(n)

✅ 2. Bottom-Up DP (2D Array)

Use a 2D dp table and fill it from the bottom up.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minimumTotal(List<List<Integer>> triangle) {
        int n = triangle.size();
        int[][] dp = new int[n][n];

        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            dp[n - 1][j] = triangle.get(n - 1).get(j);
        }

        for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
            for (int j = 0; j <= i; j++) {
                dp[i][j] = triangle.get(i).get(j) + Math.min(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i + 1][j + 1]);
            }
        }

        return dp[0][0];
    }
}

Code Explanation: This version uses a full 2D DP table to build the solution from the bottom row upwards. Each cell in the DP table stores the minimum path sum starting from that point. For each row (from bottom-1 to top), it updates each element by adding the triangle value to the minimum of the two paths directly below.

🧠 More intuitive and easier to visualize
🟡 Higher space complexity than 1D DP

Time Complexity: O(n^2)
Space Complexity: O(n^2)

✅ 3. Top-Down DP (Memoization)

Use recursion with memoization to avoid recomputation.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minimumTotal(List<List<Integer>> triangle) {
        int n = triangle.size();
        Integer[][] memo = new Integer[n][n];
        return helper(0, 0, triangle, memo);
    }

    private int helper(int i, int j, List<List<Integer>> triangle, Integer[][] memo) {
        if (i == triangle.size() - 1) {
            return triangle.get(i).get(j);
        }
        if (memo[i][j] != null) return memo[i][j];

        int left = helper(i + 1, j, triangle, memo);
        int right = helper(i + 1, j + 1, triangle, memo);

        return memo[i][j] = triangle.get(i).get(j) + Math.min(left, right);
    }
}

Code Explanation: This approach uses recursion with memoization. It starts from the top element and recursively computes the minimum path sum for both possible next moves (same index and next index). It stores intermediate results in a memoization table to avoid redundant calculations.

📌 Combines the clarity of recursion with the efficiency of dynamic programming
🟠 Uses additional space for memoization and stack frames

Time Complexity: O(n^2)
Space Complexity: O(n^2) (memo + recursion stack)

❌ 4. Plain Recursion (No Memoization)

Explores all paths; inefficient for large inputs due to exponential time.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minimumTotal(List<List<Integer>> triangle) {
        return helper(0, 0, triangle);
    }

    private int helper(int i, int j, List<List<Integer>> triangle) {
        if (i == triangle.size() - 1) {
            return triangle.get(i).get(j);
        }

        int left = helper(i + 1, j, triangle);
        int right = helper(i + 1, j + 1, triangle);

        return triangle.get(i).get(j) + Math.min(left, right);
    }
}

Code Explanation: This naive recursive method explores all possible paths from top to bottom without caching results. For each step, it computes the minimum between two recursive calls, but recomputes the same subproblems multiple times.

🚫 Very inefficient for large inputs
⚠️ Exponential time complexity leads to timeout

Time Complexity: O(2^n)
Space Complexity: O(n)

Summary of Approaches

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Optimal
Bottom-Up DP (1D) O(n^2) O(n) ✅
Bottom-Up DP (2D) O(n^2) O(n^2) ✅
Top-Down Memoization O(n^2) O(n^2) ✅
Plain Recursion Exponential O(n) ❌

Conclusion The best solution in terms of space and efficiency is the 1D Bottom-Up DP, which solves the problem in-place with minimal memory usage.

Problem Statement: Number of Paths in a Matrix with K Coins¶

Given an n x n matrix such that each of its cells contains some coins, count the number of ways to collect exactly k coins while moving from the top-left corner of the matrix to the bottom-right corner. From a cell (i, j), you can only move to (i+1, j) or (i, j+1).

Example: Number of Paths in a Matrix with K Coins

Consider the following 3x3 matrix and k = 7:

Matrix:
\[
\[1, 2, 3],
\[0, 1, 1],
\[4, 2, 1]
]
  • Start at top-left cell (0,0) with 1 coin.
  • Allowed moves: right or down.
  • Goal: Reach bottom-right cell (2,2) collecting exactly 7 coins total.

Possible paths and their coin sums:

  1. Path: (0,0) → (0,1) → (0,2) → (1,2) → (2,2)

    • Coins collected: 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 8 (too many)

  2. Path: (0,0) → (1,0) → (2,0) → (2,1) → (2,2)

    • Coins collected: 1 + 0 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 8 (too many)

  3. Path: (0,0) → (1,0) → (1,1) → (1,2) → (2,2)

    • Coins collected: 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 (too few)

  4. Path: (0,0) → (0,1) → (1,1) → (2,1) → (2,2)

    • Coins collected: 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 7 (exactly k)

  5. Path: (0,0) → (1,0) → (2,0) → (2,1) → (2,2)

    • Coins collected: 1 + 0 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 8 (too many)

Result:

  • There is exactly 1 path that collects exactly 7 coins (Path #4).
  • So, the number of ways = 1.

Constraints

  • You must collect exactly k coins.
  • Movement is only allowed to the right or downward.

Approach 1: Recursive Backtracking (Brute Force) Code

class Solution {
    long ans;
    void helper(int[][] arr, int k, int i, int j) {
        if (k < 0) return;
        if (i >= arr.length || j >= arr.length) return;
        if (i == arr.length - 1 && j == arr.length - 1 && k == arr[i][j]) ans++;
        helper(arr, k - arr[i][j], i + 1, j);
        helper(arr, k - arr[i][j], i, j + 1);
    }

    long numberOfPath(int n, int k, int [][]arr) {
        ans = 0;
        helper(arr, k, 0, 0);
        return ans;
    }
}

Code Explanation: This method explores every possible path recursively, subtracting the current cell's coins from the remaining k at each step. It terminates if k becomes negative or indices go out of bounds. When reaching the bottom-right cell, it checks if the remaining coins equal the cell’s coins and increments the count.

  • Time Complexity: Exponential (O(2^(2n))) because each step branches into two paths.
  • Space Complexity: O(n) for the recursion stack depth

Time Complexity

  • Exponential: O(2^(2n))

Space Complexity

  • O(n) for recursion stack.

Approach 2: Memoization (Top-Down DP)

Idea

Store the result of subproblems using a 3D DP array: dp[i][j][k] - number of ways to reach bottom-right from (i, j) with exactly k coins left.

Code

class Solution {
    Long[][][] dp;
    
    long dfs(int[][] arr, int i, int j, int k) {
        if (i >= arr.length || j >= arr.length || k < 0) return 0;
        if (i == arr.length - 1 && j == arr.length - 1)
            return k == arr[i][j] ? 1 : 0;

        if (dp[i][j][k] != null) return dp[i][j][k];

        long right = dfs(arr, i, j + 1, k - arr[i][j]);
        long down = dfs(arr, i + 1, j, k - arr[i][j]);

        return dp[i][j][k] = right + down;
    }

    long numberOfPath(int n, int k, int[][] arr) {
        dp = new Long[n][n][k + 1];
        return dfs(arr, 0, 0, k);
    }
}

Code Explanation: To optimize the brute force method, this approach stores results of subproblems in a 3D DP array dp[i][j][k], representing the number of ways to reach the end from (i, j) with exactly k coins remaining. It avoids recomputing overlapping subproblems by checking the memo before recursion.

  • Time Complexity: O(n^2 * k) since each state is computed once.
  • Space Complexity: O(n^2 * k) for memoization storage.

Approach 3: Bottom-Up Dynamic Programming (Tabulation)

Idea

Build a 3D DP table iteratively.

Code

class Solution {
    long numberOfPath(int n, int k, int[][] arr) {
        long[][][] dp = new long[n][n][k + 1];

        if (arr[0][0] <= k) dp[0][0][arr[0][0]] = 1;

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                for (int coins = 0; coins <= k; coins++) {
                    if (i > 0 && coins >= arr[i][j])
                        dp[i][j][coins] += dp[i - 1][j][coins - arr[i][j]];
                    if (j > 0 && coins >= arr[i][j])
                        dp[i][j][coins] += dp[i][j - 1][coins - arr[i][j]];
                }
            }
        }
        return dp[n - 1][n - 1][k];
    }
}

Code Explanation: This iterative method builds a 3D DP table from the start (0,0) to the end (n-1, n-1). For each cell and each possible coin count, it adds the number of ways to reach that state either from the top or the left, given the coins collected. The final answer is stored in dp[n-1][n-1][k].

  • Time Complexity: O(n^2 * k) due to iterating over all cells and coin counts.
  • Space Complexity: O(n^2 * k) to store all states.

Summary

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Notes
Brute Force Exponential O(n) Not efficient for large n
Memoization O(n^2 * k) O(n^2 * k) Efficient and recommended
Tabulation O(n^2 * k) O(n^2 * k) Iterative and clear

Problem Statement: Minimum Falling Path Sum¶

Given an n x n array of integers matrix, return the minimum sum of any falling path through matrix. A falling path starts at any element in the first row and chooses the element in the next row that is either directly below or diagonally left/right. Specifically, the next element from position (row, col) will be:

  • (row + 1, col - 1)
  • (row + 1, col)
  • (row + 1, col + 1)

Example Input:

matrix = [
  [2,1,3],
  [6,5,4],
  [7,8,9]
]

Output:

13

Explanation: The falling path with minimum sum is 1 → 4 → 8 = 13.

Constraints

  • n == matrix.length == matrix[i].length
  • 1 <= n <= 100
  • -100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100

Approaches ✅ 1. Bottom-Up DP with 1D Space Optimization

Iterate from bottom to top, and only maintain one row at a time.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minFallingPathSum(int[][] matrix) {
        int n = matrix.length;
        int[] dp = matrix[n - 1].clone(); 

        for (int row = n - 2; row >= 0; row--) {
            int[] newDp = new int[n];
            for (int col = 0; col < n; col++) {
                int down = dp[col];
                int left = col > 0 ? dp[col - 1] : Integer.MAX_VALUE;
                int right = col < n - 1 ? dp[col + 1] : Integer.MAX_VALUE;

                newDp[col] = matrix[row][col] + Math.min(down, Math.min(left, right));
            }
            dp = newDp;
        }

        int min = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int val : dp) {
            min = Math.min(min, val);
        }

        return min; 
    }
}

Code Explanation:

  • Initialize a 1D dp array with the values from the bottom row.
  • Iterate upwards from the second-last row to the top.
  • For each element, calculate the minimum sum by considering three possible moves from the next row: directly below, diagonally left, or diagonally right.
  • Update dp to store these minimal sums for the current row.
  • After processing all rows, the minimum value in dp corresponds to the minimum falling path sum.
  • This approach optimizes space by reusing a single 1D array.

Time Complexity: O(n^2)
Space Complexity: O(n)

✅ 2. Bottom-Up DP with 2D Table

Use a 2D table and fill from bottom to top.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minFallingPathSum(int[][] matrix) {
        int n = matrix.length;
        int[][] dp = new int[n][n];

        for (int col = 0; col < n; col++) {
            dp[n - 1][col] = matrix[n - 1][col];
        }

        for (int row = n - 2; row >= 0; row--) {
            for (int col = 0; col < n; col++) {
                int down = dp[row + 1][col];
                int left = col > 0 ? dp[row + 1][col - 1] : Integer.MAX_VALUE;
                int right = col < n - 1 ? dp[row + 1][col + 1] : Integer.MAX_VALUE;

                dp[row][col] = matrix[row][col] + Math.min(down, Math.min(left, right));
            }
        }

        int min = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int val : dp[0]) {
            min = Math.min(min, val);
        }

        return min;
    }
}

Code Explanation:

  • Use a 2D dp array of the same size as the matrix.
  • Initialize the last row of dp with the last row of the matrix.
  • For each cell from bottom to top, calculate the minimum path sum using the three possible next positions.
  • The answer is the minimum value in the first row of dp.
  • This approach explicitly keeps the minimum sums for each cell in a 2D structure.

Time Complexity: O(n^2)
Space Complexity: O(n^2)

✅ 3. Top-Down DP (Memoization)

Use recursion with memoization to avoid recomputation.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minFallingPathSum(int[][] matrix) {
        int n = matrix.length;
        Integer[][] memo = new Integer[n][n];

        int minSum = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int col = 0; col < n; col++) {
            minSum = Math.min(minSum, dfs(0, col, matrix, memo));
        }
        return minSum;
    }

    private int dfs(int row, int col, int[][] matrix, Integer[][] memo) {
        if (col < 0 || col >= matrix.length) return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        if (row == matrix.length - 1) return matrix[row][col];
        if (memo[row][col] != null) return memo[row][col];

        int down = dfs(row + 1, col, matrix, memo);
        int left = dfs(row + 1, col - 1, matrix, memo);
        int right = dfs(row + 1, col + 1, matrix, memo);

        memo[row][col] = matrix[row][col] + Math.min(down, Math.min(left, right));
        return memo[row][col];
    }
}

Code Explanation:

  • Use recursion to explore all possible paths starting from the top row.
  • Memoize results in a 2D memo array to avoid redundant calculations.
  • For each cell, recursively compute the minimal falling path sum by checking down, diagonal left, and diagonal right.
  • Return the minimal sum found from the top row.
  • This approach avoids recomputation with memoization.

Time Complexity: O(n^2)
Space Complexity: O(n^2) (memo + recursion stack)

❌ 4. Plain Recursion

Brute-force all paths. Not feasible for large inputs.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minFallingPathSum(int[][] matrix) {
        int n = matrix.length;
        int minSum = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int col = 0; col < n; col++) {
            minSum = Math.min(minSum, dfs(0, col, matrix));
        }
        return minSum;
    }

    private int dfs(int row, int col, int[][] matrix) {
        if (col < 0 || col >= matrix.length) return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        if (row == matrix.length - 1) return matrix[row][col];

        int down = dfs(row + 1, col, matrix);
        int left = dfs(row + 1, col - 1, matrix);
        int right = dfs(row + 1, col + 1, matrix);

        return matrix[row][col] + Math.min(down, Math.min(left, right));
    }
}

Code Explanation:

  • Recursively explore all paths starting from the top row without memoization.
  • For each position, recursively check the three possible next steps.
  • This brute force approach examines all falling paths.
  • Not efficient for large n due to exponential complexity.

Time Complexity: O(3^n)
Space Complexity: O(n)due to recursion stack.

Summary of Approaches

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Optimal
Bottom-Up DP (1D) O(n^2) O(n) ✅
Bottom-Up DP (2D) O(n^2) O(n^2) ✅
Top-Down Memoization O(n^2) O(n^2) ✅
Plain Recursion Exponential O(n) ❌

Conclusion For best efficiency, use the Bottom-Up DP with 1D space optimization approach. It's fast and uses minimal space.

Problem Statement: Minimum Falling Path Sum II¶

Given an n x n integer matrix grid, return the minimum sum of a falling path with non-zero shifts. A falling path with non-zero shifts is a choice of exactly one element from each row such that no two elements chosen in adjacent rows are in the same column.

Example Input:

grid = [
  [2,1,3],
  [6,5,4],
  [7,8,9]
]

Output:

13

Explanation:
Choose 1 (row 0, col 1) → 4 (row 1, col 2) → 8 (row 2, col 1) = 13.
We ensure no two selected elements are in the same column in adjacent rows.

Constraints

  • n == grid.length == grid[i].length
  • 1 <= n <= 200
  • -99 <= grid[i][j] <= 99

Approaches ✅ 1. Optimized DP (Track First & Second Min Values)

This is the optimal approach. At each row, keep track of the smallest and second smallest values from the previous row. For each column, if the column index equals the index of the minimum, take the second minimum instead.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minFallingPathSum(int[][] grid) {
        int n = grid.length;
        int[] dp = new int[n];
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) dp[j] = grid[0][j];

        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
            int[] newDp = new int[n];
            int min1 = Integer.MAX_VALUE, min2 = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
            int min1Index = -1;
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                if (dp[j] < min1) {
                    min2 = min1;
                    min1 = dp[j];
                    min1Index = j;
                } else if (dp[j] < min2) {
                    min2 = dp[j];
                }
            }
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                if (j == min1Index) {
                    newDp[j] = grid[i][j] + min2;
                } else {
                    newDp[j] = grid[i][j] + min1;
                }
            }

            dp = newDp;
        }

        int result = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int val : dp) {
            result = Math.min(result, val);
        }

        return result;
    }
}

Code Explanation:

  • Use a 1D DP array to store minimum sums for each column of the current row.
  • For each row, identify the smallest (min1) and second smallest (min2) values from the previous DP row along with the index of the smallest (min1Index).
  • For each column in the current row:
    • If the column matches min1Index (i.e., same column as previous minimum), add min2 to the current cell value.
    • Otherwise, add min1.
  • Update DP array after processing each row.
  • The result is the minimum value in the DP array after processing all rows.
  • This approach avoids the costly O(n³) search for minimum in previous rows by precomputing the two smallest values, improving efficiency.

Time Complexity: O(n^2)
Space Complexity: O(n)

✅ 2. Classic DP with Full Table (Brute-force Column Comparison)

Try every valid column in the current row (excluding the previous row's column), and build a 2D DP table.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    public int minFallingPathSum(int[][] grid) {
        int n = grid.length;
        int[][] dp = new int[n][n];
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) dp[0][j] = grid[0][j];

        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                dp[i][j] = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
                for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) {
                    if (k != j) {
                        dp[i][j] = Math.min(dp[i][j], grid[i][j] + dp[i-1][k]);
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        int result = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            result = Math.min(result, dp[n-1][j]);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

Code Explanation:

  • Use a 2D DP array where dp[i][j] represents the minimum sum of a falling path ending at row i and column j.
  • For each cell, iterate over all columns in the previous row except the current column to find the minimum sum path that doesn't repeat the column.
  • This results in three nested loops causing O(n³) time complexity.
  • Simpler to understand but inefficient for large inputs.

Time Complexity: O(n^3)
Space Complexity: O(n^2)
⚠️ Slower for large n.

✅ 3. Top-Down DP with Memoization

Use recursion with memoization and skip the previous column.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    int[][] memo;
    int[][] grid;
    int n;

    public int minFallingPathSum(int[][] grid) {
        this.n = grid.length;
        this.grid = grid;
        this.memo = new int[n][n];
        for (int[] row : memo) Arrays.fill(row, Integer.MAX_VALUE);

        int result = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            result = Math.min(result, dfs(0, j, -1));
        }

        return result;
    }

    private int dfs(int row, int col, int prevCol) {
        if (col == prevCol) return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        if (row == n - 1) return grid[row][col];
        if (memo[row][col] != Integer.MAX_VALUE) return memo[row][col];

        int min = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int nextCol = 0; nextCol < n; nextCol++) {
            if (nextCol != col) {
                min = Math.min(min, dfs(row + 1, nextCol, col));
            }
        }

        return memo[row][col] = grid[row][col] + min;
    }
}

Code Explanation:

  • Use recursion to explore all falling paths starting from the top row.
  • Pass along the previous column index to ensure the next choice differs in column.
  • Use a memoization table to store results for (row, col) to avoid repeated computations.
  • For each recursive call, try all columns except the previous column.
  • This reduces the recomputation but still involves O(n³) worst-case due to three nested dimensions: row, col, and previous column exclusion.

Time Complexity: O(n^3) worst-case
Space Complexity: O(n^2) + recursion stack

Summary

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Notes
Optimized DP (min1, min2) O(n^2) O(n) ✅ Best performance
Full DP Table (Brute-force) O(n^3) O(n^2) ❌ Slower, simple to understand
Top-Down with Memoization O(n^3) O(n^2) ✅ Recursive solution

Conclusion To handle this problem efficiently, the optimized DP using min1, min2 tracking is the best approach with O(n^2) time and space efficiency.

Problem Statement: Subset Sum Problem¶

Given an array of positive integers arr[] and a value sum, determine if there is a subset of arr[] with a sum equal to the given sum.

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 1000
  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000
  • 1 ≤ sum ≤ 1000

Example Input:

arr[] = {3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2}
sum = 9

Output:

true

Explanation:

  • There is a subset with sum 9: {4, 5}.

Approaches

1. Dynamic Programming (Tabulation) We can solve this problem using dynamic programming by creating a 2D DP array dp[i][j] where dp[i][j] is true if a subset with sum j can be made using the first i elements.

Java Code:

class Solution {

    static Boolean isSubsetSum(int arr[], int sum) {
        int n = arr.length;
        boolean[] prev = new boolean[sum + 1];
        boolean[] curr = new boolean[sum + 1];
        prev[0] = true;

        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j <= sum; j++) {
                if (j < arr[i - 1]) {
                    curr[j] = prev[j];
                } else {
                    curr[j] = prev[j] || prev[j - arr[i - 1]];
                }
            }
            System.arraycopy(curr, 0, prev, 0, sum + 1);
        }
        return prev[sum];
    }
}

Explanation:

  • We maintain two arrays, prev and curr, to keep track of possible subset sums for each value in the array.
  • The prev array stores the results from the previous row, while the curr array stores the current row’s results.
  • Initially, prev[0] is set to true because we can always form the sum 0 (by selecting no elements).

Time Complexity:

  • O(n * sum) where n is the number of elements in the array, and sum is the target sum.

Space Complexity:

  • O(sum) due to the space used by the prev and curr arrays.

2. Recursive Approach (Brute Force)

In a brute force approach, we recursively check if we can form the given sum by including or excluding each element from the array.

Java Code:

class Solution {

    static Boolean isSubsetSum(int arr[], int n, int sum) {
        if (sum == 0) return true;
        if (n == 0) return false;

        // If last element is greater than sum, it cannot be included
        if (arr[n - 1] > sum) {
            return isSubsetSum(arr, n - 1, sum);
        }

        // Check if sum can be obtained by including or excluding the last element
        return isSubsetSum(arr, n - 1, sum) || isSubsetSum(arr, n - 1, sum - arr[n - 1]);
    }
}

Explanation:

  • The base cases are:
    • If the sum is 0, we can form the sum by not including any elements.
    • If we have no elements left and the sum is not 0, we cannot form the sum.
  • At each recursive step, we either include or exclude the current element.

Time Complexity:

  • O(2^n) due to the exponential nature of the recursive calls.

Space Complexity:

  • O(n) due to the recursion stack.

3. Memoization (Top-Down Dynamic Programming)

We can optimize the recursive approach by using memoization to store the results of already computed subproblems.

Java Code:

class Solution {

    static Boolean isSubsetSum(int arr[], int n, int sum) {
        Integer[][] dp = new Integer[n + 1][sum + 1];
        return isSubsetSumMemo(arr, n, sum, dp);
    }

    static Boolean isSubsetSumMemo(int arr[], int n, int sum, Integer[][] dp) {
        if (sum == 0) return true;
        if (n == 0) return false;

        if (dp[n][sum] != null) return dp[n][sum];

        // If last element is greater than sum, it cannot be included
        if (arr[n - 1] > sum) {
            dp[n][sum] = isSubsetSumMemo(arr, n - 1, sum, dp) ? 1 : 0;
        } else {
            dp[n][sum] = (isSubsetSumMemo(arr, n - 1, sum, dp) || isSubsetSumMemo(arr, n - 1, sum - arr[n - 1], dp)) ? 1 : 0;
        }

        return dp[n][sum] == 1;
    }
}

Explanation:

  • We store results of subproblems in the dp table to avoid redundant calculations.
  • The table is initialized with null values, and for each subproblem, we check if it has already been solved.

Time Complexity:

  • O(n * sum) due to the memoization table.

Space Complexity:

  • O(n * sum) for the dp table.

4. Space Optimized Dynamic Programming

Instead of maintaining a 2D DP table, we can optimize the space by using only a 1D array, since we only need the previous row at each step.

Java Code:

class Solution {

    static Boolean isSubsetSum(int arr[], int sum) {
        int n = arr.length;
        boolean[] dp = new boolean[sum + 1];
        dp[0] = true;

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = sum; j >= arr[i]; j--) {
                dp[j] = dp[j] || dp[j - arr[i]];
            }
        }

        return dp[sum];
    }
}

Explanation:

  • We use a single array dp[] where dp[j] represents whether a subset with sum j is possible.
  • We iterate over the array in reverse order to avoid overwriting values that might be needed later in the same iteration.

Time Complexity:

  • O(n * sum), similar to the tabulation approach.

Space Complexity:

  • O(sum), as we are using only a 1D array.

Summary of Approaches

Approach Time Complexity Space Complexity Suitable For Large n
Brute Force (Recursive) O(2^n) O(n) ❌
Memoization (Top-Down DP) O(n * sum) O(n * sum) ✅
Dynamic Programming O(n * sum) O(sum) ✅
Space Optimized DP O(n * sum) O(sum) ✅✅

Conclusion

  • Dynamic Programming (Tabulation or Space Optimized) is the most efficient approach for this problem, with a time complexity of O(n * sum).
  • Brute Force (Recursive) is not suitable for larger inputs due to its exponential time complexity.
  • Memoization offers a middle ground, improving the recursive approach by avoiding redundant calculations.

Problem Statement: Perfect Sum Problem¶

Given an array arr of non-negative integers and an integer target, the task is to count all subsets of the array whose sum is equal to the given target.

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 1000
  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000
  • 1 ≤ target ≤ 1000

Example Input:

arr[] = {1, 2, 3}
target = 4

Output:

2

Explanation:

  • The subsets of {1, 2, 3} that sum to 4 are {1, 3} and {2, 2}.

Approaches

1. Dynamic Programming (Tabulation) We can solve this problem using dynamic programming, similar to the subset sum problem. We maintain a DP table dp[i][j] where dp[i][j] will store the number of subsets that can form the sum j using the first i elements of the array.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    // Function to calculate the number of subsets with a given sum
    public int perfectSum(int[] arr, int target) {
        int n = arr.length;
        int[] prev = new int[target + 1];
        int[] curr = new int[target + 1];
        prev[0] = 1; // There's one way to form sum 0 (by choosing no elements)

        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            System.arraycopy(prev, 0, curr, 0, target + 1);
            for (int j = 0; j <= target; j++) {
                if (j >= arr[i - 1]) {
                    curr[j] += prev[j - arr[i - 1]];
                }
            }
            System.arraycopy(curr, 0, prev, 0, target + 1);
        }
        return curr[target];
    }
}

Explanation:

  • We maintain two arrays, prev and curr. The prev array stores the results of the previous row, and curr stores the results for the current row.
  • The logic behind the tabulation is to check if we can include or exclude the current element to form the sum.
  • We initialize prev[0] = 1 because there is one way to form sum 0 (by selecting no elements).

Time Complexity:

  • O(n * target), where n is the number of elements in the array and target is the target sum.

Space Complexity:

  • O(target), as we only maintain two arrays of size target + 1.

2. Recursive Approach (Brute Force) In the brute force approach, we recursively check if we can form the given target sum by including or excluding each element in the array.

Java Code:

class Solution {
    // Function to calculate the number of subsets with a given sum
